Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural police stations
Comments: Rural police stations in Guinea (Police Nationale/Gendarmerie) record case files, complaints, and incidents using handwritten paper-based procès-verbaux (PVs), as per standard francophone African practice and Guinea's Code de Procédure Pénale. The 2018 MSPC Police Statistical Yearbook reports 8,843 PVs drawn up nationwide (including rural CCPs/DRPs like N'Zérékoré, Faranah), based on manual registers/fiches; rural challenges include poor archiving, no computers or vehicles. The Innovatrics ABIS in Conakry digitises paper criminal records/fingerprints centrally, with regions sending paper for central processing — this does not constitute digital recording at rural facility level. US State Dept HR reports (2023/2024) describe manual detentions with no digital recording at stations. No rural-specific digital evidence found; entirely paper-based at point of service.

revised_comments: Rural police stations in Guinea (Police Nationale and Gendarmerie) continue to record case files, complaints and criminal proceedings (procès-verbaux) by hand on paper, in line with the Code de Procédure Pénale. The 2018 Ministry of Security and Civil Protection statistical yearbook records thousands of manually compiled procès-verbaux nationwide, including in rural commissariats and gendarmerie brigades, based on paper registers. The national Automated Biometric Identification System, supplied by Innovatrics, digitises fingerprint and criminal records centrally in Conakry, with regional stations still submitting material on paper for central processing rather than capturing data digitally at the point of service. As of late 2025, government announcements on new police infrastructure describe plans to introduce digital operational management systems only from 2026 onwards, indicating that routine data capture at police facilities, particularly in rural areas, remains entirely paper-based.

Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural civil registry offices
Comments: Rural registry offices in Guinea primarily use paper-based systems for birth registration. Vital events like births occurring at home are first recorded in paper "village notebooks" by local sector chiefs and then forwarded to the head of the rural commune (mayor or delegate), who serves as the official registrar and issues certificates manually (UNICEF Profile; UNECA Snapshot). Processing is explicitly "manually (on paper)." Limited digital elements exist in isolated pilots and some urban/commune centers: a 2017 modernization pilot in rural N’zerekore region introduced computers (standalone, not networked); an EU-backed project (2021-2024) in 10 municipalities digitizes existing paper records into a national database post-recording; ~40 centers acquiring computers with local backups planned. No evidence of digital tools at point-of-service in most rural facilities or networked systems for routine use (UNECA Snapshot; Enabel Project). Key barriers: poor accessibility (centers often >5km from villages), untrained volunteer staff, lack of electricity/connectivity, large backlog (>25% unregistered births). National CRVS Reform Strategy (2018-2022) aims at modernization/DHIS2 linkage, but rural point-of-service remains paper-dominant, with digital limited to aggregation/pilots—not shifting majority to digital recording.

The UNICEF CRVS profile (fln.dk) confirms the legacy paper-based, decentralised mayoral registration process; the two other originally cited sources (UNECA snapshot, citizenshiprightsafrica) could not be fetched (repeated timeouts) so are not relied upon further. Fresh, well-corroborated primary government sources show that since April 2025 the government has run the Programme National de Recensement Administratif a Vocation d'Etat Civil (PN-RAVEC), a nationwide biometric civil-status enrolment campaign using computers and biometric kits deployed to enrolment centres across the country, including rural prefectures (e.g. around 300 centres in rural Mandiana prefecture), feeding a new National Civil Status Register (RNEC) under an April 2025 decree that explicitly permits paper or electronic declaration by registrars. This is genuine evidence of a shift towards digital capture, but PN-RAVEC is a census-style enrolment campaign rather than confirmed proof that routine, day-to-day rural civil registry office operations (recording new births/deaths as they occur) are now digitised, so this is flagged for human review rather than asserted with full confidence.
revised_comments: Civil registration in rural Guinea has historically relied on paper-based recording: vital events are first noted in paper village registers by local chiefs and then transmitted to the commune registrar (mayor or delegate) for manual certification. Since April 2025, the government has rolled out the Programme National de Recensement Administratif a Vocation d'Etat Civil (PN-RAVEC), a nationwide biometric enrolment campaign that captures civil-status facts (births, marriages, deaths, adoptions) digitally using computers and fingerprint/iris scanners deployed to hundreds of enrolment centres, including in rural prefectures such as Mandiana, which alone hosted around 300 centres. The programme feeds a new National Civil Status Register (RNEC), and its implementing decree allows registrars to record events on paper or electronically. This represents a genuine, though still developing, shift towards digital capture in the civil registration system, alongside earlier EU-backed pilots (2021-2024) and computer provision in around 40 centres, with paper registers continuing to be used for routine registration in most rural offices.

Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary schools
Comments: Rural primary schools in Guinea use paper-based registers for recording administrative data, attendance, and learning outcomes. National EMIS exists with data aggregated by the National Institute of Statistics into yearbooks, but collection at rural facilities remains entirely manual, later transcribed at higher levels. A World Bank project (BOSIB, closed 2024) piloted tablets for ~25,000 primary teachers and mobile data entry, but failed to achieve its targets: 0% of schools achieved digital data integration or dashboard usage. The GIGA/UNICEF connectivity project (2025-2026) aims to connect 2,200 schools but is prospective. Only 35% of primary schools have electricity. No evidence of any functioning digital recording system at rural school level; the failed pilot with 0% adoption does not constitute digital presence at point of service.

revised_comments: Rural primary schools in Guinea continue to record attendance, enrolment and learning-outcome data on paper. The World Bank-financed Early Childhood and Basic Education project, which closed with an Implementation Completion Report in January 2024, piloted tablets and mobile data entry for around 25,000 primary teachers, but the government ultimately cancelled the disbursement-linked results requiring school-level information to be entered via mobile technology and integrated into a national database for at least 90 percent of schools, and requiring dashboards to be used by at least 20 percent of decision-makers. The GIGA/UNICEF connectivity initiative, launched in November 2025, aims to connect 2,200 public primary schools to the internet by the end of 2026, with around 600 schools equipped so far, but this addresses internet access rather than digital administrative data capture. No evidence indicates a functioning digital record-keeping system at the rural school level; data capture at the point of service remains entirely paper-based.

Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary healthcare clinics
Comments: Rural primary healthcare clinics in Guinea predominantly use paper-based systems for patient data recording, including registers and forms for routine care and initial surveillance reporting. Aggregate weekly disease data and individual case notifications are compiled on paper at clinics/health centers and sent to District Health Offices for digital entry into DHIS2, which is used nationally for surveillance and routine monthly reporting since 2016.Implementation of DHIS2 for Disease Surveillance in Guinea. No evidence of widespread point-of-care digital systems like EMRs in government rural clinics; Swiss Re Foundation notes pre-project reliance on paper.Swiss Re Foundation on Clinic+O. Digital pilots exist, e.g., Clinic+O NGO deploys offline EMRs and dashboards in select rural CHCs/community outreach, integrating with national systems via manual uploads; successful but limited scale.Oxford Open Digital Health study. Barriers: poor connectivity/electricity, staff shortages/training gaps, infrastructure lacks. National policy pushes DHIS2 post-Ebola, but rural point-of-service remains paper; digital for district aggregation only. Score 2 reflects paper default with isolated donor pilots, not majority routine use.

A Gavi-funded evaluation found that, as of March 2022, only 59 of 444 health centres nationwide had implemented the electronic logistics management system for vaccine stock, of which just 4 were rural. A PASA2/Ministry of Health programme report shows computer kits and solar power were provided mainly to district-level structures (hospitals, prefectural health directorates) rather than to primary rural clinics, where paper primary registers continue to be reproduced and disseminated. The Swiss Re Foundation Clinic+O project, launched in late 2025, explicitly frames rural community health centres as reliant on paper-based systems today. No change to score.
revised_comments: Rural primary healthcare clinics in Guinea predominantly record patient data on paper. Weekly aggregate disease-surveillance data and individual case notifications are compiled on paper at health centres before being entered into DHIS2 at district level, the national platform used since 2018 for routine reporting. A Gavi-funded evaluation found that, as of March 2022, only 59 of 444 health centres nationwide had implemented the electronic logistics management information system for vaccine stock, of which just four were rural, with paper vaccine registers remaining the norm elsewhere. The Clinic+O initiative, an NGO-led programme launched in late 2025 with Swiss Re Foundation support, is digitising data collection at selected rural community health centres using offline electronic medical records and tablets, integrating with the national health information system, while explicitly describing rural centres as currently reliant on paper-based systems. This combination of a paper-based default with limited, growing digital pilots at facility level supports a status of mostly paper with some digital capture.
